site.name: Where Did the Day Go?
site.tagline: Time zones, explained so a 10-year-old gets it.
meta.home.title: Where Did the Day Go? — Time Zones Explained for Kids
meta.home.description: Pick any two cities on Earth and see the time difference explained with live clocks, a day ribbon and a flight simulator. Simple enough for a 10-year-old.
meta.route.title: {from} to {to} Time Difference — Explained Simply
meta.route.description: {to} is {gap} {direction} {from}. See live clocks for both cities, what time it is there right now, and why you lose or gain a day when you fly.
home.intro: Two cities are almost never on the same clock. Pick any two and see exactly how far apart they are — and what a flight does to a whole day.
home.pick.noResults: No city matches that. Try another name.
home.why.title: Why this site exists
home.why.body: Most tools give you a number. This one shows what it means: what your family is doing right now on the other side of the world, and why a long flight can land you two days later.
route.subtitle.same: {to} and {from} are on the same clock
route.lede.ahead: When it is breakfast time in {from}, {to} is already well into its {toPart}. Here is what that actually looks like.
route.lede.same: These two cities keep the same time all year, so there is nothing to work out — but the flight still takes a while.
clocks.title: Two cities, two clocks
clocks.note: These are the real times right now. Watch the seconds tick. Look at the sky behind each clock — when one city is bright, the other is usually dark.
clocks.sentence.differentDay: {toCity} is already on {toDay} while {fromCity} is still on {fromDay}.
ribbon.kicker: The same moment, two different days
ribbon.title: Slide through a whole day
ribbon.note: Each stripe is 24 hours in one city. They are lined up so everything in the same vertical column happens at exactly the same instant. Drag the slider — or tap straight on the stripes.
ribbon.note.halfHour: Look closely at the bottom stripe: its blocks do not line up with the ones above, because this city's clock is half an hour off from most of the world.
ribbon.note.quarterHour: Look closely at the bottom stripe: its blocks sit three quarters of an hour off the ones above — one of the rarest clock settings on Earth.
arc.title: The longest nap of your life
arc.note: A nonstop plane between {from} and {to} would fly for roughly {hours} — that is an estimate from the distance, and real flights vary with aircraft, winds and routing.
arc.note.polar: The short way round a ball is not the way it looks on a flat map: this route climbs to about {lat}° latitude before coming back down.
arc.schoolDays: That is roughly {n} school days in one seat.
sim.title: Pick a takeoff time
sim.note: Choose when you leave and the app does the time-zone maths for you — including which day you land on.
sim.dstSkip: {time} does not exist today — the clocks jumped!
sim.verdict.forward: You take off at {depTime} on {depDay} and land at {arrTime} on {arrDay}. Count that on a calendar and {calendar} went by — but you were only in the air {flight}. The extra {gap} is the jump you make when you set your watch to {toCity} time. That is the chunk of the day people mean when they say you lose a day flying east.
sim.verdict.back: Almost a magic trick. You leave at {depTime} on {depDay} and land at {arrTime} on {arrDay} — the clock only moved {calendar}, even though you flew for {flight}. Flying this way hands you back {gap}.
sim.verdict.same: You take off at {depTime} on {depDay} and land at {arrTime} on {arrDay}. Both cities keep the same clock, so the landing time is simply the takeoff time plus the {flight} you spent in the air.
why.title: Three things grown-ups get wrong
why.halfHour.title: Why do some clocks end in :30?
why.halfHour.body: Most countries set their clock by a line of longitude. India picked one exactly between two zones, so its clock lands on :30. Nepal is even odder: :45.
why.oneZone.title: One clock for a whole country
why.oneZone.body: India is 3,000 km wide but keeps one clock — the sun rises almost two hours earlier in the east than the west. China does the same across an even wider span.
why.dst.title: The gap keeps changing
why.dst.body: Some places shift their clocks twice a year and some never do. When only one of your cities shifts, the gap changes too. This page reads today's real gap live.
why.dst.bodyBoth: Both cities change their clocks for daylight saving, but not on the same date — so for a few weeks a year the gap is different. This page reads it live.
why.dst.bodyNeither: Neither city ever changes its clocks, so this gap stays the same all year — unusual for a long-haul route.
jetlag.title: Why the first few nights feel upside down
jetlag.note: Your body clock doesn't get on the plane with you — it only shifts about an hour a day, and this trip moves you {gap}. The first three or four nights feel the strangest.
jetlag.tip1.title: Change your watch at takeoff.
jetlag.tip1.body: Start thinking in the new city's time before you even land.
jetlag.tip2.title: Get outside in the morning.
jetlag.tip2.body: Daylight is the main signal your brain uses to reset its clock.
jetlag.tip3.title: Drink lots of water.
jetlag.tip3.body: Plane air is drier than a desert, and being thirsty makes jet lag feel worse.
jetlag.tip4.title: Stay up until bedtime.
jetlag.tip4.body: A giant nap on landing day is the fastest way to be wide awake at 3 a.m.
faq.title: Common questions
faq.q1: What is the time difference between {from} and {to}?
faq.q2: What time is it in {to} when it is noon in {from}?
faq.a2: When the clock says 12:00 noon in {from}, it is {noonTime} in {to}.
faq.q3: How long is the flight from {from} to {to}?
faq.a3: The two cities are about {km} km apart in a straight line over the Earth's surface, which works out at roughly {hours} of flying nonstop. Real flights take longer when they stop on the way.
faq.q4: Do you lose a day flying from {from} to {to}?
faq.a4: Flying east you set your watch forward, so the calendar moves further than the hours you actually spend in the air — that is the day people say they lose. Flying back west you set it backwards and get those hours returned.
faq.q5: Does the time difference between {from} and {to} change during the year?
faq.dst.onlyFrom: {from} changes its clocks for daylight saving and {to} does not, so the gap shifts by an hour for part of the year.
faq.dst.onlyTo: {to} changes its clocks for daylight saving and {from} does not, so the gap shifts by an hour for part of the year.
faq.dst.both: Both cities use daylight saving, but they usually switch on different dates — so for a few weeks each year the gap is an hour off its usual value.
faq.dst.neither: No. Neither city changes its clocks, so this gap holds all year round.

footer.body: Clock offsets and daylight-saving rules come from your device's own IANA time-zone database, read live, so they stay correct when the rules change. Distances are great-circle (straight-line over the Earth's surface). Flight times are estimates from that distance, not airline timetables.
